---

**What the double-date normally means**

In England, the civil year began on 25 March (Lady Day) rather than 1 January. Because of that, any date falling between 1 January and 24 March belonged to two different years depending on which reckoning you used: the Old Style year (still in force under the English calendar) and the New Style year (already ticked over by modern, 1-January reckoning). Clerks resolved the ambiguity by writing both years separated by a slash — for example, "6 January 1745/6" means 1745 by Old Style but 1746 by New Style.

---

**Why 25 March is different — and why this slash is anomalous**

The double-date window is **1 January through 24 March only**. On 25 March itself, the Old Style year increments: the outgoing year ends and the incoming year begins on that very day. The Old Style year and the New Style year therefore agree on 25 March, leaving nothing to resolve with a slash. A slash written on 25 March is anomalous.

---

- **1750** — if the clerk was still treating 25 March as the closing day of the outgoing year at the moment of writing
- **1751** — if the register had already turned over at Lady Day and the clerk was recording the incoming year

The date as written does not settle which. **Do not record either 1750 or 1751 as definitive yet.**

Record whichever year the register's own practice supports, and note in your research file that the slash on 25 March was anomalous.
